clue.text: Some prang started causing anxiety

indicators.note: 'Some' asks for only part of what follows, so the answer is a piece cut from the next words.

parts.note: The letters run across the gap, starting after the P-R of prang and ending before the rest of started.

explanation.surface: A minor car bump leaves the driver rattled.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'prang' is British slang for a small car crash, which is what makes the surface sound natural; the letters straddle the gap between its two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Angst is the German loanword for a deep, nagging anxiety, and English uses it as a straight synonym.

clue.text: Ron in no trouble as it's easily laundered

indicators.note: Letters 'in trouble' are in disorder, so they get rearranged.

parts.note: The eight letters of RON IN NO, rearranged.

explanation.surface: Ron has no worries about the washing because it comes out of the machine without fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: The little word 'in' looks like it places Ron somewhere, but it is part of the letters to shuffle, and 'no' reads as a word rather than fodder too.
explanation.definitionFit: Non-iron fabric dries smooth and needs no pressing, which is exactly what makes it easy to launder.

clue.text: Odd spider near Tuscan city

indicators.note: 'Odd' points at the odd-numbered positions, so take the first, third, fifth letters and so on.

parts.note: The first, third and fifth letters of spider.
The first and third letters of near, carrying the count on.

explanation.surface: A strange spider is lurking close to an Italian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' reads as 'strange' in the surface, describing the spider, and the letter run carries on into 'near' rather than stopping at the end of the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Siena is the walled hill city in Tuscany, famous for its Palio horse race.

clue.text: Woman finds happiness at church

parts.note: Joy is happiness.
CE is the Church of England.

explanation.surface: A woman discovers contentment through her faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Woman' is a crossword signal for a girl's name, and CE for 'church' is one of the most common abbreviations in the genre.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce is a woman's first name, and a name like this is defined by the broad class it belongs to.

clue.text: A politician's after gold for public speaking

indicators.note: 'After' says the politician comes later than the gold, so the gold is written first.

parts.note: OR is gold in heraldry, from the French.
The article, kept as it is.
A Tory is a British Conservative politician; the 's is 'is', joining the pieces.

explanation.surface: A politician chasing gold medals in debating.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', not a possessive, and it reads 'a politician is after gold'. OR for gold comes from heraldry.
explanation.definitionFit: Oratory is the art of public speaking, especially the formal, eloquent kind.

clue.text: Grass on Catholic leader for beliefs

indicators.note: 'On' means added on to, so the grass is attached after the other piece.
A leader stands at the front, so the leader of a word is its first letter.

parts.note: The first letter of Catholic.
A reed is a tall grass of wet ground.

explanation.surface: Someone informs on the head of the Catholic church because of his faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass on' is British slang for informing on someone, and the surface leans on it; here 'grass' is simply a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A creed is a set of religious beliefs, from the Latin 'credo', I believe.

clue.text: Coming in first if frozen rigid

indicators.note: Something 'coming in' is inside, so the answer sits within the words that follow.

parts.note: The run begins with the last two letters of first, takes all of if, and ends on the opening letter of frozen.

explanation.surface: Someone arriving first is frozen stiff with cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First' tempts you to count positions or write 1ST, but it only lends its last two letters to the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Stiff and rigid are plain synonyms: both describe something that will not bend.

clue.text: Like little photo of jelly

parts.note: 'Like' and 'as' both mean in the manner of.
A pic is a short word for a picture or photo.

explanation.surface: A small snapshot of a wobbly dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' signals a shortened word here, PIC being the clipped form of picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspic is a savoury jelly made from meat or fish stock, used to set cold dishes.

clue.text: Hope Ravel piece is musical drama

indicators.note: A piece is a part of a whole, so the answer is a part of the words before it.

parts.note: The run starts after the H of Hope and stops two letters into Ravel.

explanation.surface: A work by the composer Ravel described as a stage piece with music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece' pretends to be a musical composition by Ravel, which suits the surface perfectly; it is the instruction to take a piece of 'Hope Ravel'.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera is a drama set to music and sung throughout.

clue.text: Weight of cask, say

indicators.note: 'Say' means spoken aloud, so the answer is a word that sounds like the one before it.

parts.note: A tun is a large cask for wine or beer; said aloud it gives a metric weight.

explanation.surface: Asking how heavy a barrel is.
explanation.walkthrough: TUN is an old word for a big barrel, worth keeping because setters use it often.
explanation.definitionFit: A tonne is the metric unit of weight equal to a thousand kilograms.

clue.text: Push pea around and become fit

indicators.note: Letters moved around are shifted into a new order.

parts.note: The seven letters of PUSH PEA, rearranged.

explanation.surface: A fussy eater nudges a pea about the plate and hopes to get healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Push' looks like an instruction to move the pea, but it is fodder alongside it; 'around' works on both words together.
explanation.definitionFit: To shape up is to get into good physical condition, which is what becoming fit means.

clue.text: Prestigious car, rarer model in Formula One

indicators.note: To model something is to shape it, so the letters get reshaped.
'In' places one thing inside another, so the reshaped letters go between the others.

parts.note: The first letter of Formula, as on the F1 badge.
RARER, rearranged.
One is I in Roman numerals, the other half of F1.

explanation.surface: A luxury car described as a very rare model in motor racing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' passes for a car model in the surface; it is the rearranging instruction. Formula One shortens to F1, and the 1 becomes I.
explanation.definitionFit: Ferrari is the Italian maker of expensive sports cars, the byword for a prestige car.

clue.text: More rum and Pernod derived inside

indicators.note: 'Inside' says the answer is within the words just named.

parts.note: The run takes the last two letters of Pernod and the first three of derived.

explanation.surface: More spirits and aniseed liqueur taken in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' wants to be the drink, keeping company with Pernod; it is the old adjective meaning strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Rum is a British informal adjective for strange or peculiar, so more rum means odder.

clue.text: Agreement with penultimate element

parts.note: An element is a unit, one of the parts that make up a whole.
Y is the penultimate letter of the alphabet, just before Z.

explanation.surface: A deal involving the second-to-last chemical element.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penultimate' seems to describe the element, but on its own it points to the alphabet's next-to-last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Unity is a state of agreement or harmony between people.

clue.text: Lurching tourist

definitions.note: 'Lurching' is a participle, not a noun; the setter lets it stand for one who lurches, a person who trips.
definitions.meaning: Someone lurching is stumbling along, one who trips over their feet.
A British word for a day-tourist, someone out on a short excursion.

explanation.surface: A sightseer staggering about unsteadily.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses of 'trip' do the work: a stumble and an outing.
explanation.definitionFit: A tripper is a British word for a tourist on a short outing, and the word also describes someone who trips and lurches.

clue.text: Tokyo rebuilt another Japanese city

indicators.note: Something rebuilt is put together again differently, so the letters are reassembled.

parts.note: The five letters of TOKYO, rearranged.

explanation.surface: Tokyo is reconstructed as a second Japanese city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' is part of the definition: the answer is a Japanese city other than the one named.
explanation.definitionFit: Kyoto is Japan's former imperial capital, a city distinct from Tokyo.

clue.text: Less bland Moroccan town

definitions.meaning: The comparative of tangy: sharper and zestier, so less bland.
The port city on Morocco's side of the Strait of Gibraltar.

explanation.surface: A Moroccan town with more flavour than the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words are spelt the same but said differently: the town stresses the second syllable, the comparative the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangier means more tangy, the opposite of blander, and is also Morocco's northern port city.

clue.text: Woman coming round all right to call up

indicators.note: Coming round something means encircling it, so the woman surrounds the other piece.

parts.note: Eve, the first woman in Genesis.
OK means all right.

explanation.surface: A woman visits to phone someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming round' sounds like a friendly visit; it means the woman's name wraps around OK.
explanation.definitionFit: To evoke is to call up a memory or feeling, bringing it to mind.

clue.text: Restrict most untidy houses

indicators.note: What a phrase houses is held inside it, so the answer is lodged within those words.

parts.note: The run takes the last two letters of most and the first three of untidy.

explanation.surface: Limiting the messiest homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Houses' reads as a noun in the surface, messy homes, but it is a verb meaning contains.
explanation.definitionFit: To stunt is to restrict growth or development, as poor soil stunts a plant.

clue.text: Agree with incredible youth leader

parts.note: A tall story is an incredible one.

indicators.note: A leader goes first, so the leader of a word is its opening letter.

parts.note: The first letter of youth.

explanation.surface: Going along with an amazing leader of young people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tall' for 'incredible' comes from the phrase 'tall tale', not from height.
explanation.definitionFit: Figures that tally agree with each other, as matching records do.

clue.text: Drive out to get composer

indicators.note: 'Out' can mean wrong or disordered, so the letters are put out of their usual order.

parts.note: The five letters of DRIVE, rearranged.

explanation.surface: Heading out in the car to pick up a musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive out' reads as one phrasal verb, a trip in the car; split it and the second word works on the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Verdi was the Italian composer of Aida and La Traviata.

clue.text: Weren't for the most part moved to begin again

indicators.note: 'For the most part' means nearly all, so the word loses its last letter.
Letters moved are shifted into a new order.

parts.note: WERENT without its final T.

explanation.surface: People were not, on the whole, inspired to start over.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'weren't' is ignored, leaving WERENT, and trimming it before rearranging is the order of work.
explanation.definitionFit: To renew something is to begin it again, as with a subscription or an effort.

clue.text: Somehow I attain role of queen

indicators.note: 'Somehow' means in some way or other, so the letters are arranged in some other way.

parts.note: The seven letters of I ATTAIN, rearranged.

explanation.surface: An actor wonders how they landed the part of a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is an actor's surprise at being cast; the part in question is in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Titania is the queen of the fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream, a stage role.

clue.text: Model pleads for jobs

parts.note: The Model T was Henry Ford's famous early car.
To plead is to ask earnestly.

explanation.surface: A fashion model begs to be hired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' paints a catwalk model in the surface; crosswords use it for the letter T through the Ford Model T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasks and jobs are plain synonyms: pieces of work to be done.

clue.text: Family doctor at home of key person in organisation

parts.note: Your kin are your family.
A GP is a general practitioner, the British family doctor.
Someone at home is in.

explanation.surface: The family doctor making a house call to someone important in a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Family doctor' reads as one phrase, the British term for a GP, but 'family' is KIN on its own and 'doctor' alone gives GP.
explanation.definitionFit: A kingpin is the most important person in a group, originally the central pin in bowling.

clue.text: Pile out after spiv's initial patter

indicators.note: 'Out' can mean disordered, so the letters are knocked out of their order.
'After' puts this piece later than the one named next, so it follows it.
An initial is the first letter of a name, so only the opening letter is taken.

parts.note: The first letter of spiv.
PILE, rearranged.

explanation.surface: A dodgy dealer's sales pitch pours out in a heap.
explanation.walkthrough: A spiv is a flashy British petty crook of the post-war black market, just the sort to have a spiel, which makes the surface hang together.
explanation.definitionFit: A spiel is a glib, practised line of talk, the same as a salesman's patter.

clue.text: Second moderately hot group

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second.
Warm is moderately hot.

explanation.surface: The runner-up in a band that is only lukewarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like it describes the group; it is the unit of time, abbreviated S.
explanation.definitionFit: A swarm is a large moving group, of bees or of people.

clue.text: Unfair lending causes American rage, but not loud

parts.note: US for American.

indicators.note: 'But not' excludes something, so the named letter is taken away.

parts.note: Fury is rage.
F is forte, loud in music; it is removed from FURY.

explanation.surface: Loan sharks make Americans quietly furious.
explanation.walkthrough: F for loud comes from the musical marking forte, the opposite of P for piano, soft.
explanation.definitionFit: Usury is lending money at an unreasonably high rate of interest.
